summary: Specifies JMAP, a protocol for clients to efficiently query, fetch, and modify JSON-based data objects, with push notification of changes, fast resynchronization, and out-of-band binary upload and download. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A modern way for apps to ask a server for their data, using a common data format and quick updates.

subtitle: A generic JSON-over-HTTPS protocol for syncing mail, calendars and contacts, with batching, delta updates and push.

tldr.problem: Clients such as mobile and web apps need to keep data like mail, calendars and contacts in sync with a server while using as little network and battery as possible.
tldr.mechanism: JMAP exposes a uniform set of JSON methods (get, set, changes, query and more) over authenticated HTTPS. Many method calls can be batched in one request and can refer to each other's results, state strings let clients fetch only what changed, and a push channel signals when to resync.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8620 defines only the generic core; separate specifications define the data models for each data type. It is a Proposed Standard that has since been updated.

facts.label: Change history to keep
facts.value: SHOULD cover states given out in the last 30 days

today: RFC 8620 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9404 and RFC 9670. Data models such as mail are defined in separate specifications.

sections.title: What JMAP Is For
sections.content:
The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) is used for synchronising data, such as mail, calendars or contacts, between a client and a server. It is optimised for mobile and web environments and aims to give a consistent interface to different data types. This RFC covers only the generic mechanism; further specifications define the data models.

Three design aims run through the text. Use limited network resources efficiently: batch multiple API calls in one request, use push instead of polling, and send delta updates. Scale horizontally to very large numbers of users: separate endpoints after login, separation of binary and structured data, and a sharing model with no data dependencies between accounts. Stay uniform: every data type is created, read, changed and deleted with the same family of methods.

All data except binary uploads and downloads is I-JSON (a strict subset of JSON) encoded in UTF-8. All HTTP requests MUST use https:// and MUST be authenticated. Ids are server-assigned, immutable strings of 1 to 255 octets from the URL-safe base64 alphabet without padding.
sections.eli5: It is a tidy way for your apps to ask a server for your stuff, like email and calendar, without wasting battery on a lot of back-and-forth chatter.

sections.title: Accounts, Users and Records
sections.content:
A user is a person accessing data. An account is a collection of data that can hold many data types, such as mail, contacts and calendars. An account is not the same as a user: a shared work calendar or a support-desk mailbox is an account that several users may access, and one set of credentials can reach several accounts. Most methods take a mandatory accountId.

A data type is a named set of typed properties, like a table schema, and each instance is a record. A record's id must be unique among records of the same type within the same account, but may clash across accounts or types.

If a severe internal error forces a server to reallocate ids, it MUST treat that as the account being deleted and recreated with a new account id, so clients throw away old data and refetch.
sections.eli5: An account is like a shared filing cabinet. Several people can have keys to the same cabinet, and one person can have keys to several cabinets.

sections.title: The Session Resource and Discovery
sections.content:
To connect, a client needs the URL of the Session resource and credentials. A successful authenticated GET returns a JSON Session object with capabilities, accounts, primaryAccounts, username, apiUrl, downloadUrl, uploadUrl, eventSourceUrl and a state string. Clients MUST ignore properties they do not understand.

The urn:ietf:params:jmap:core capability MUST be present and carries the server's limits, with suggested minimums: maxSizeUpload 50,000,000, maxConcurrentUpload 4, maxSizeRequest 10,000,000, maxConcurrentRequests 4, maxCallsInRequest 16, maxObjectsInGet 500 and maxObjectsInSet 500, plus the supported collationAlgorithms. Other capabilities, including vendor extensions identified by a URL on the vendor's own domain, extend the protocol, and a client MUST opt in to each one it uses.

Autodiscovery: a host for example.com SHOULD publish a DNS SRV record _jmap._tcp.example.com (usually port 443), and the Session resource is then at https://${hostname}[:${port}]/.well-known/jmap. Because the Session may change, implementors are told to disable HTTP caching of it.
sections.eli5: First you ask the server for a map of what it offers and where each door is. After that you know which door to use for questions, for files, and for news.

sections.title: Batched Requests and Result References
sections.content:
An API request is an authenticated POST of application/json to apiUrl, holding one Request object. Its using array lists the capabilities wanted, and methodCalls is an array of Invocations: each is a three-element array of method name, arguments object and a client-chosen method call id. The server MUST process the calls sequentially, in order, and returns a Response with methodResponses in the same order and a sessionState.

To save round trips, an argument may be taken from an earlier call's result. The client prefixes the argument name with a hash sign and gives a ResultReference with resultOf, name and path. The path is a JSON Pointer that also allows an asterisk to map through an array. If a reference fails to resolve, the method is rejected with invalidResultReference. The RFC's example fetches the sender, date and subject of the Emails in the first 10 Threads of an inbox in four chained calls in one request.

Errors come at three levels. A whole request can be rejected with an HTTP error and a problem-details body (for example unknownCapability, notJSON, notRequest or limit). An individual method can fail with an error response such as unknownMethod or invalidArguments, which MUST NOT cause an HTTP-level error, and later calls still run. Individual records in a set can fail with a SetError. Calls from different concurrent requests may interleave, so data can change between two calls of one request.
sections.eli5: You hand the server a list of jobs in one envelope, and a later job can say 'use whatever the first job found'. If one job fails, the others still get done.

sections.title: The Standard Methods
sections.content:
For a data type Foo, JMAP defines the same set of methods, and a type's specification says which ones it has.

  • Foo/get fetches records by ids (null means all, within maxObjectsInGet) and returns a state string for all data of that type in the account, plus list and notFound.
  • Foo/changes takes a sinceState and returns created, updated and destroyed ids, a newState and hasMoreChanges. A server SHOULD be able to calculate changes from any state string given to a client in the last 30 days; otherwise it returns cannotCalculateChanges and the client MUST invalidate its cache.
  • Foo/set creates, updates and destroys records. Updates are PatchObjects keyed by JSON Pointer paths, so a client may send just keywords/chopin: true. Each record change is atomic, but the server may commit some and reject others, reporting notCreated, notUpdated and notDestroyed. An optional ifInState aborts with stateMismatch if the data changed. New records get temporary creation ids that later calls can reference with a hash-sign prefix.
  • Foo/copy is the only way to move records between accounts: copy, then optionally destroy the original with onSuccessDestroyOriginal. The two steps are not atomic.
  • Foo/query and Foo/queryChanges search, sort and window large data sets on the server and then update a cached query, using filter (AND, OR, NOT operators), sort comparators, position or anchor, limit and queryState.
sections.eli5: For every kind of thing there are the same few buttons: fetch, what changed, change it, copy it, and search. Learn them once and they work for mail, calendars and everything else.

sections.title: Binary Data: Upload and Download
sections.content:
Files are kept out of the JSON API. Binary data is referred to by a blobId, which stands only for the raw immutable bytes; the name and content type live in the object that references it. Any blobId in an account may be reused when creating or updating another object in that account, for instance to attach an old message to a new one without downloading and re-uploading it.

To upload, the client POSTs to the uploadUrl template (which MUST contain accountId) and gets back accountId, blobId, type and size. To download, it GETs the downloadUrl template filled in with accountId, blobId, type and name. Since the data never changes, long cache times are recommended, for example Cache-Control: private, immutable, max-age=31536000. Blob/copy copies blobs between accounts server side.

An unreferenced blob (every upload starts as one) MAY be deleted by the server, but not for at least 1 hour after upload except to enforce quota, and it is visible only to the uploader. Servers SHOULD apply a separate quota to unreferenced blobs.
sections.eli5: Big files, like photos, go through a separate loading door. You get a claim ticket for each one and can hand that ticket over later instead of carrying the file again.

sections.title: Push Notifications
sections.content:
Push is deliberately minimal: the server sends a StateChange object that maps each changed account id to the new state string of each changed data type. The client compares those with its own and, if they differ, fetches the details with the /changes methods. Several changes can be coalesced, and lost pushes do no harm because the next get or set reveals the change.

There are two delivery routes.

  • Event source: the client holds open a GET to the eventSourceUrl (a text/event-stream resource). The URL template has types, closeafter (state or no) and ping variables. The server pushes a state event and SHOULD send an event id so a reconnecting client's Last-Event-ID shows what it missed. Servers MUST NOT have a minimum ping interval higher than 30 or a maximum lower than 300 seconds.
  • PushSubscription: the client registers an https:// URL, and the server POSTs each notification there, so any push service can carry it. The subscription may carry client-generated keys for encryption under RFC 8291, a list of types and an expires time. For subscriptions tied to non-expiring credentials the maximum expiry MUST be at least 48 hours and SHOULD be at least 7 days.

To stop the server being used to attack a third party, on creation the server immediately POSTs a PushVerification with a verification code and MUST NOT send anything further until the client updates the subscription with that code.
sections.eli5: The server does not send the news itself, only a little knock that says 'something changed in your mail'. You then ask for the details yourself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All requests MUST use TLS 1.2 or later following the recommendations of RFC 7525, servers SHOULD support TLS 1.3, and clients MUST validate certificate chains. The RFC says use of HTTP Basic authentication is NOT RECOMMENDED, and where used, a unique app password per client is strongly recommended so access can be revoked per device.

SRV-based autodiscovery is open to DNS poisoning unless secured by something like DNSSEC, so servers must make sure the /.well-known/jmap path cannot be controlled by an attacker. Servers MUST implement sensible limits against resource exhaustion, since a small request can cause a very large response. For push, the server MUST ensure the URL is externally resolvable to avoid server-side request forgery, MUST limit how many subscriptions a user has and how fast they are created, and a client using a third-party push service MUST specify encryption keys. The RFC also notes that the timing of requests and pushes can leak information to a passive observer.
sections.eli5: Everything travels in a locked tube, the server limits how much any one person can ask for, and it double-checks before knocking on any new door.
